args.content:
# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy (v2, Nov 2026)

## Constraints (these come first)
- **People:** Morgan (evenings/weekends, writing, okay Python). Possible volunteer: Priya Raman (data analyst, ~5 hrs/week).
- **Money:** at most $2,000 of Morgan's savings in 2026. Payments need Morgan's explicit approval.
- **Public profile:** Morgan's name is kept off anything public (posts, open letters, press, public comments, published site) until Morgan has talked to Dorrance HR (employment agreement s.7; outside-activities disclosure due 30 Nov).

## What we're actually good for
A one-person project won't change frontier lab decisions directly. Where it can help is in neglected, well-scoped work that has a clear audience. The best fit for our skills (writing, Python, data analysis) is **careful measurement and clear write-ups**. That kind of work has a high ratio of usefulness to resources, and other people can check it and build on it.

## Recommended focus: one small, public-good eval project
Pick one property that nobody is measuring systematically and that matters for safety. Build a small open benchmark or tracking dataset, run it on publicly available models over time, and write up the results honestly, including limits and null results.

Candidate topics (to narrow down with Morgan and Priya):
1. **Consistency of model self-reports.** Do models' stated policies and capabilities match how they behave on matched tasks? Run it across versions.
2. **Tracking safety claims made in model releases.** Build a structured, versioned dataset of what labs say in system cards (evals run, thresholds, mitigations), so changes over time can be seen. This is data-analyst-friendly and needs almost no compute.
3. **Small replications.** Re-run published safety eval results on open-weight models to check whether they hold up.

My recommendation is **#2 first**. It's cheap and useful to governance people right away, Priya's skills fit it, and it doesn't depend on compute credits. #1 or #3 can follow once compute credits are in hand.

## Funding
- **Emberfall Fund rapid grants** (closes 30 Nov, $5k–$25k). Morgan must be the named, accountable applicant. A draft is in `grants/emberfall-rapid-draft.md`, for Morgan to review after the HR conversation.
- **Compute Commons** rolling credits. Apply later if we pursue #1 or #3.
- Personal budget use so far: $0.

## Not doing (for now)
- Signing open letters, press quotes, or public docket comments under Morgan's name. Revisit after HR.
- Launching a newsletter. There are already plenty.
- Paying for Pagewell Pro. The free subdomain is fine until there's something to show.

## Next 30 days
1. Morgan: talk to HR; renew the domain; decide on the grant.
2. Define the schema for the release-claims dataset (`project/release-claims/README.md`).
3. Onboard Priya with a scoped first task.
4. Once there are 10 or more releases coded, write a short methods note. Publish it only when Morgan is cleared to be named, or publish it anonymously as the org if Morgan prefers.

# Release Safety Claims Tracker (working title)

**Question:** When frontier developers release a model, what do they claim about safety testing, and how do those claims change over time and differ between developers?

## Unit of analysis
One row per (model release × claim). Sources: system/model cards, safety frameworks, release blog posts. Primary sources only, archived (Wayback link plus a local PDF/HTML snapshot).

## Draft schema (`claims.csv`)
| field | description |
|---|---|
| release_id | e.g. `devname-modelname-YYYYMMDD` |
| developer | organisation |
| release_date | ISO date |
| source_url | primary source |
| archive_url | Wayback snapshot |
| claim_category | one of: dangerous-capability-eval, alignment-eval, third-party-testing, threshold/commitment, mitigation, deployment-restriction, other |
| domain | e.g. bio, cyber, autonomy, persuasion, n/a |
| claim_text | short verbatim quote (≤ 50 words) |
| quantitative | y/n: does it report a number? |
| external_party | named third-party evaluator, if any |
| verifiable | y/n/partial: could an outsider check it? |
| coder | initials |
| notes | free text |

## Process
- Two coders double-code 20% of rows. Report agreement.
- Coding guide in `CODING_GUIDE.md` (to be written after a 5-release pilot).
- Stick to describing what was claimed. Don't make accusations, and keep any interpretation in clearly separated write-ups.

## First task (suggested for a volunteer)
Pilot: code 5 recent releases from 3 different developers using the schema above. Note every place where the schema doesn't fit.

# DRAFT: Emberfall Fund rapid grant proposal
_Status: draft for Morgan's review. Not submitted. Deadline 30 Nov 2026. Morgan must be the named applicant, so check with Dorrance HR first (outside-activities disclosure)._

## What we'll do
Build and maintain an open, versioned dataset of the safety claims frontier AI developers make when they release models: which evaluations they report, which thresholds and commitments they state, which third parties tested the model, and whether outsiders can verify any of it. Over six months we will code every major release from at least five developers since 2024, publish the dataset and coding guide openly, and write two short analyses showing how practices are changing.

## Why it matters
Policymakers, journalists and researchers keep asking "what did the lab actually say it tested?", and the answer is spread across PDFs that change over time. A structured, archived record makes it easy to compare developers and track commitments over time. It costs little and doesn't depend on access to the labs.

## Why us
[Morgan: 2–3 sentences on your background. Writing, Python, and why you started Halcyon Threshold.] A volunteer data analyst has offered ongoing help [confirm with Priya before naming her].

## Deliverables (6 months)
- Public dataset (CSV + archived sources) covering at least 40 releases
- Coding guide with inter-coder agreement reported
- Two short write-ups (~1,500 words each)
- A refresh process so the dataset stays current

## Budget (draft: $9,500)
| item | cost |
|---|---|
| Part-time research/coding time (Morgan, ~6 hrs/week × 26 weeks at $40/hr, rounded) | $6,200 |
| Stipend for volunteer coder (Priya, if she wants one) | $2,000 |
| Hosting, domain, archiving tools | $300 |
| Contingency / small API costs for spot-checks | $1,000 |
| **Total** | **$9,500** |

_Note: paid time may count as "paid outside work" under the Dorrance agreement, so confirm with HR._
